summary: Cast-iron skeleton tower on the south end of Anclote Key, lit 15 September 1887 and deactivated in the mid-1980s; relit in 2003 and now climbable on open-house days.

access.note: Boat access only. Tower open to climbers at Friends of Anclote Key open houses (10:00 am to 4:00 pm on the second weekend of each month, October to May; donation requested).

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends gives the focal plane as 101 feet, and the USLHS place record gives 101 ft focal height (30.78 m). The station record's 34 m, from Wikidata, does not match either. Verify against the current Light List before applying.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 2003 date in the record is the relighting after the restoration (ceremony 13 September 2003). The 1887 date is the first lighting of the original tower. The record's two first-light dates both refer to this tower, one before and one after its dark years.
Not resolved. LighthouseFriends gives 1984 (the USLHS archive also says discontinued 1984); the nomination says 1985, decommissioned and abandoned.

The nomination's 'keeper Robert E. Meyer' (Spanish-American War passage) and the roster's and Service Bulletins' Robert S. Meyer are printed as different names. The sources do not say whether they are one man, so the story does not join them.

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left standing in the story: (1) deactivation 1984 (LighthouseFriends; the USLHS place record says Year Discontinued 1984) vs 1985 (nomination); the story gives both. (2) Fuel and lamp: kerosene from 1887 until the early 1940s (nomination) vs incandescent oil vapor, listed in the 1912 Service Bulletin among stations changed (Anclote Keys, Fla.) vs automatic acetylene in 1923 (LighthouseFriends). The story says the nomination's dates conflict with both. (3) Automation: 1952 (LighthouseFriends) vs the 1960s 250-watt electric light (nomination). The nomination also says the Coast Guard took over operation in the early 1940s and the Lighthouse Service merged into the Coast Guard in 1939; the story reports the 1939 merger only. (4) Lens and signal: 1898 fourth-order replacement (nomination) vs 1899 red-flash signature change (LighthouseFriends) vs 1917 change from single to triple flash (Service Bulletin 1917, OCR poor; checked against the OCR text 'Anclote Keys ... from sing le nash to triple f1asb', not against the page image). (5) Keeper name: the nomination's 'keeper Robert E. Meyer' (Spanish-American War) vs the roster's and the 1913 Bulletin's Robert S. Meyer; the story does not join them. (6) Sponge captain: the nomination's John Corcoris (co-founder of the Sponge Exchange with Cheyney) vs LighthouseFriends' John M. Cocoris (hired by Cheyney for sponge work). The story says the sources do not say whether they are the same man. (7) Focal height: 101 ft (30.8 m; LighthouseFriends and USLHS place record) vs 34 m (station record; not traceable to a cited source). The story gives the focal plane in feet only. (8) The 1896 storm: the Light-House Board report dates the storm 'September 28 and 30, 1896' in the Arbutus passage and 'September 28 and 29, 1896' in the Cedar Keys passage; the story gives both. The 1896 Anclote repair is a single sentence in the tender's report (the Arbutus paragraph), not a detailed account. The 1918 storm and rescues are from the Service Bulletin 1918 (PDF pp. 54-56); a Tarpon Springs newspaper search for 1918 produced no readable match and local press coverage is not used. The two logbook entries (1889 and 1890) are quoted from LighthouseFriends, which prints them from the station log; the original log was not read. The 1928 job description is LighthouseFriends' quotation; its source document was not read. Visiting information is taken from the Friends' open-house page as read on 22 October 2026; the state park page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. The Friends' page also describes Friday boat service by a commercial operator (Odyssey Cruises) and charters on weekends; the story does not name operators and says only that the Friends do not run boats. The 'Robert E. Meyer' cannon story is undated apart from the Spanish-American War period. Keepers' roster lines carry USLHS person slugs as printed by roster.py --json. Modern volunteers and staff are not named. Moody died in January 1925 (LighthouseFriends); the story does not say so. The Commissioner's 1919 list also credits Moody; the story uses the 1918 Bulletin and LighthouseFriends for the same rescue. Distance: LighthouseFriends gives 'three miles offshore' from Tarpon Springs; the story keeps the miles as printed because no nautical-mile figure is sourced.
